content.title: About
content.content: Fat‑free coffee creamer powder is designed to enhance the flavor and texture of coffee. It dissolves in hot or cold beverages, giving them a creamy smoothness without adding fat calories.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Powdered fat‑free creamer is commonly used in office coffee machines for quick drink preparation.
The formula usually contains skim milk solids, emulsifiers and flavorings, which create a stable foam.
Lack of fat makes the product suitable for low‑calorie diets.
Some versions are fortified with B‑vitamins and calcium.
The powder has a long shelf life when kept dry.

items.title: Reduced calorie intake
items.content: Absence of fat allows you to lower the energy content of coffee without sacrificing taste.

items.title: Calcium enrichment
items.content: Skim milk solids provide an additional source of calcium, beneficial for bone health.

items.title: Convenient use
items.content: The powder dissolves quickly, saving time when preparing drinks.

items.title: Supports low‑fat eating patterns
items.content: Ideal for people monitoring fat consumption or following low‑fat diets.

items.title: Flavor stability
items.content: Emulsifiers keep the taste consistent even after prolonged storage.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Contains skim milk solids, which may trigger reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Artificial flavorings
items.content: Some variants include synthetic flavorings that may not be preferred by all consumers.

items.title: Excess additives
items.content: Overuse could lead to excessive intake of emulsifiers and stabilizers.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Add 1‑2 teaspoons of powder to hot or cold coffee and stir until fully dissolved. It works well in lattes, cappuccinos, mochas, and even cold brew drinks.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a sealed container in a dry, cool place away from direct sunlight. Moisture can cause the powder to clump and lose its solubility.

content.title: About
content.content: Cucumber salad is made from fresh cucumbers sliced thinly and dressed with a mixture of vinegar, salt, sugar, and spices. It is a light dish often served as an appetizer or side in Eastern European and Asian cuisines.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cucumbers are about 95 % water, giving the salad a high hydration level.
Vinegar in the dressing helps keep the cucumbers crisp even after several hours.
Traditional Russian “oguretsky salad” often adds dill and mustard, but the basic recipe uses only vinegar and spices.
Cucumber salad is commonly served in hot weather because it refreshes and helps lower body temperature.
Some regions add a touch of honey to balance the acidity of the vinegar.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The high water content of cucumbers supports the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Low Calorie
items.content: Cucumber salad is very low in calories, making it ideal for weight‑management diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Cucumbers provide vitamin B6 and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: The skin of cucumbers contains quercetin, a compound with anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: Digestive Support
items.content: Vinegar stimulates stomach acid production, aiding digestion.

items.title: Cucumber allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to cucumbers.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Large amounts of vinegar can irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If salt is added to the dressing, total sodium intake should be monitored.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Improperly washed cucumbers may carry pathogens; they should be rinsed thoroughly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled as a standalone snack or as a side to meat dishes. It can be kept in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days, allowing the flavors to meld.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the salad in an airtight container in the fridge. Over time cucumbers may lose their crunch, so it’s best to consume within 48 hours.

potato-roasted-from-fresh-peel-not-eaten.title: Potato, roasted, from fresh, peel not eaten, made with oil

content.title: About
content.content: Potato is a tuber obtained from the roots of the plant Solanum tuberosum. Roasted potatoes are prepared from fresh tubers, the peel is usually not eaten, and they are cooked in vegetable oil. They feature a crispy crust and a soft, aromatic interior.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potatoes were introduced to Europe from South America in the 16th century.
There are more than 4,000 potato varieties differing in colour, shape and taste.
Frying in oil increases calorie content but retains most B‑vitamins.
Potato peel is rich in fiber and polyphenols, but it is omitted in this product.
Potatoes are among the most widely consumed foods worldwide.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Roasted potatoes provide a notable amount of potassium, which supports heart and muscle function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: They contain vitamins B6 and B3, which are involved in metabolism.

items.title: Energy supply
items.content: Carbohydrates give a quick source of energy.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Frying creates compounds such as carotenoids that have antioxidant activity.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: Even without the peel, the flesh supplies a modest amount of dietary fiber that aids bowel regularity.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Cooking in oil markedly raises the calorie count, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: The added vegetable oil increases total fat intake, which may be undesirable for certain diets.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: High‑temperature frying can produce acrylamide, a potentially harmful compound; avoid over‑cooking.

items.title: Oil allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to the type of oil used.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Roasted potatoes are served as a side dish, fries, wedges or cubes. They can be seasoned with salt, spices, or herbs. For a healthier option, use olive or sunflower oil and avoid over‑frying.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked roasted potatoes in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat in an oven or skillet to restore crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Ramen soup is a traditional Japanese dish consisting of wheat‑flour noodles served in a flavorful broth. This version includes water added to the dry noodle packet, allowing a quick, complete ramen to be prepared at home.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Ramen originated in China but became popular in Japan in the early 20th century.
Dry ramen kits often contain spices, dried vegetables, and meat pieces.
The added water activates gluten in the noodles, giving them a firm, chewy texture.
There are more than 30 regional broth styles: shoyu, miso, shio, and tonkotsu.
In Japan ramen is considered street food, and many cities have dedicated ramen bars.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Ramen noodles provide fast‑acting carbs that quickly replenish energy.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Dry mixes often include dried chicken or pork protein, boosting the protein content.

items.title: Minerals from broth
items.content: Seasoning packets can supply sodium, potassium, and magnesium, important for electrolyte balance.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat flour and spices provide modest amounts of B1, B2, and niacin.

items.title: Convenient preparation
items.content: Adding water and a short boil yields a hot meal in minutes, ideal for time‑pressed situations.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Dry ramen kits are often very salty, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Wheat‑based noodles are unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Additives and flavor enhancers
items.content: Some kits contain artificial flavors and MSG, which may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The dish can be calorie‑rich, especially when topped with fatty ingredients.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bring 500 ml of water to a boil, add the dry noodles and cook for 3‑4 minutes. Then stir in the seasoning packet and let sit for 1‑2 minutes. Optionally top with a boiled egg, sliced green onions, nori, or meat slices.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the dry ramen kit in a sealed package in a cool, dry place. After opening, transfer to an airtight container to prevent moisture absorption.

turkey-light-and-dark-meat-roasted-skin-.title: Turkey, light and dark meat, roasted, skin eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Turkey is a large bird native to North America. Roasted turkey meat, both light (breast) and dark (thighs, drumsticks), is often enjoyed with the skin, which becomes crisp and flavorful when properly cooked. The meat is high in protein, low in fat, and versatile for many dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkeys were domesticated by Native Americans over 2,000 years ago.
Light meat (breast) contains less fat than dark meat, but both are rich in B‑vitamins.
When roasted to a golden crust, turkey skin provides healthy fatty acids and a savory aroma.
Roasted turkey is a centerpiece of Thanksgiving in the United States, but it is popular worldwide.
Turkey meat is easily digested and often recommended in weight‑loss diets.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving of roasted turkey provides about 29 g of high‑quality protein, essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Light meat contains less than 2 g of fat per 100 g, making it suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Turkey supplies niacin (B3), vitamin B6 and B12, which support energy metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Minerals: selenium, zinc, phosphorus
items.content: These minerals are important for immune health, bone strength, and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Favorable cholesterol profile
items.content: Dark meat has slightly more fat than breast but still lower than red meat, which can be beneficial for cholesterol levels.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked turkey may harbor Salmonella; cook to an internal temperature of 74 °C (165 °F).

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to turkey proteins.

items.title: Sodium in processed products
items.content: Prepared roasted turkeys are often seasoned with salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: High purine content
items.content: Dark meat is relatively high in purines, which can be a concern for gout sufferers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Roasted turkey can be sliced for sandwiches, added to salads, soups, or served as a main course with sides. The crisp skin can be eaten as a snack or used to enrich broths.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool roasted turkey to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 3–4 days. For longer storage, freeze in freezer‑safe bags at –18 °C (0 °F) for up to 2–3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 74 °C before serving.
